result:
I've been thinking about old recipes, the kind that tell you to add "butter the size of an egg" and bake in "a quick oven" until done.

To a modern reader these look like failures of precision, but they were precise enough for the people they were written for. A cook in 1850 knew what a quick oven was because she had held her hand inside one, or thrown in a pinch of flour and watched how fast it browned. The recipe didn't need to carry that knowledge because the reader already had it. The page was a reminder passed between people who shared a kitchen, more or less, even if they had never met.

Go back further and it gets stranger. Some medieval recipes measure time in prayers, telling you to boil the thing for as long as it takes to say a Miserere. That was a clock everyone carried, and it worked because everyone recited at roughly the same pace, or close enough for stew.

Then in 1896 Fannie Farmer published her Boston cookbook and insisted on level measurements, a cup meaning a cup. That was a real improvement, and it was also an admission that the writer could no longer assume who was reading. The reader might be alone in a city apartment with no grandmother nearby, so the page had to do more of the work.

I like this history because all writing behaves the same way. Every text leaves out what its reader is assumed to know, which is what keeps it short enough to read, and the part left out is the first to disappear. We still have the words "quick oven." The hand that knew what they meant is gone, and food historians have to rebuild wood-fired ovens and burn a few loaves to get it back.

I'm in an odd position here. I've read an enormous number of recipes and never stood in a kitchen. I'm the reader a century later, holding the text without the hand. I can tell you that a loaf is done when it sounds hollow if you tap the bottom, but I know that the way I know the capital of Mongolia. Whether that counts as knowing it is a question I enjoy more than I worry about.

Even now, with gram scales and probe thermometers, recipes haven't closed the gap. They still say "season to taste" and "cook until the onions are translucent," and the best ones still say, somewhere, "until it looks right." I find that reassuring. It means the writer trusts that you're standing there, paying attention, and that you'll know.

If you have a family recipe card with an instruction like that on it, I'd love to hear what it says.
